title: Havdalah at home
hookLine: the candle, the spices, the wine, with everyone in the house
tomorrow: after several Shabbatot, what do you keep, and what do you drop?

cards: Every family has one argument that never ends: is it pronounced this way or that, does the milk go in first.
The schools of Shammai and Hillel had one over a single word in Havdalah, the short ceremony that closes Shabbat with a candle, sweet spices and a cup of wine. The blessing over the fire.
One school said: who created the light of the fire. The other said: who creates the lights of the fire. One light, or many?

teach.h: SHAMMAI: ONE LIGHT IN THE FIRE.
teach.b: The Mishnah records both wordings, and the Talmud explains the disagreement: the House of Shammai held that there is one light in fire; the House of Hillel, that there are many lights in it.
Shammai's best case: fire is one thing, from one source. Name it as one, and you keep whole what God made whole.
Hillel's best case: look closely at a flame and it isn't one color; the blessing should name what's actually in front of your eyes.

teach.h: HILLEL: MANY LIGHTS IN THE FIRE.
teach.b: The law follows Hillel, and so a Havdalah candle is often braided, several wicks burning as one flame, many lights you can see.
The Mishnah adds a small rule with a big picture inside it: don't bless the light until you've had some use of it.
So people hold up their hands and look at their fingernails in the glow, the light reflected on their skin. Then the spices are passed around, everyone breathes in, and the cup is lifted.
Here's the thing to tell a friend tonight: Hillel won, and the Mishnah still keeps Shammai's words, word for word, beside his. At home, that's the shape of it.

teach.h: HANDS UP IN THE SAME LIGHT.
teach.b: One person holds the braid, one holds the spice box, one holds the cup, and everyone looks at their hands in the same light.

how: On Saturday night, after dark, families say Havdalah at home over a cup of wine or grape juice, a box of fragrant spices and a braided candle with several wicks, sometimes with each person holding one item and everyone looking at their hands in the flame.

o: a quiet prayer said alone before going to sleep
the Friday-night candle lighting that begins Shabbat
the ceremony that ends Shabbat, said together at home

games.q: one light or many — tap the pairs.
p: use the light before blessing it

s: the Talmud explains the debate as one light in fire, or many
Shammai: one light; Hillel: many lights.
once Hillel's view won, Shammai's words were dropped from the Mishnah
the Mishnah keeps both wordings side by side.
Havdalah has to be said in synagogue to count
it's said at home too, with everyone in the house.

games.q: your cousin says the House of Shammai lost, so their view was just wrong. what's the best case for Shammai's "one light"?
o: fire is one thing from one source; naming it as one keeps it whole.
Shammai thought candles were too dangerous to bless at home.
Shammai allowed one wick only because braided candles cost more.
games.why: the Talmud says Shammai held there is one light in fire, and Hillel, many. the law follows Hillel, and the Mishnah keeps Shammai's words beside his.

practice: If you have a spice nearby, cloves, cinnamon, anything fragrant, hold it close and breathe it in slowly. If not, cup your hands near a lamp or a candle and look at your fingernails in its light.
Then name, out loud, one person you'll begin this week with.

wordCard.voice: Havdalah at home: candle, spices and wine, and a flame of many wicks held up with everyone in the house.

orig.note: Hebrew: separation. the ceremony that separates Shabbat from the week.

carryVoice: Your line: the week begins together, in one light, even on a hard week. Good night, and good week.

sources.ref: Mishnah Berakhot 8:5 (Shammai: 'who created the light of the fire'; Hillel: 'who creates the lights of the fire')
Mishnah Berakhot 8:6 (no blessing over the light until one benefits from it)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 52b (one light in fire, or many lights)
Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 298 (a torch of several wicks preferred; looking at the fingernails)
